title: Recall by meaning: a local embedding model as a second channel, summaries first, lookup before every Bash command as an option
description: User (2026-11-09), after the measurements on a real store: asked 'Shall I build the semantic channel on EmbeddingGemma as an opt-in setup (about 1.5 GB per machine with its runtime), used for prompts and failed commands, with word matching kept for exact ids? ... summary-first delivery would go in with it', he answered: 'yes, build it, and enable it on this machine by default. 1.5s is also very much fine to run before every bash process, make it a configuration option please'. Earlier the same day: 'I want relevant memories to be fetched in based on a prompt or a tool call', 'we need a very good search of the memories that are relevant to the prompt - I think we need to have some sort of semantic similarity measure. What can be used locally WITHOUT any external API calls?', 'We are OK to download a few GB of model and use up a few seconds for the command lookup + CPU cycles', and 'We want to be as lean as possible'. Why this model: on the real store it was the only method that beat the shipped word matching on every column (see the comments on ck-3jk).

comments.author: siler
comments.text: Built, enabled on this machine, not committed or released (the tree is at 1.6.0 with a CHANGELOG entry, waiting for the user's word to commit, tag and push). What exists: hooks/recall.py (the model runner, its setup with a pinned revision and sha256 checks, the switches in $CREW_HOME/recall.json, a per-project vector cache, two lock slots so at most two models are in memory at once) and bin/crew-recall (setup, status, set, test, index). hooks/memories.py: merge() orders found-by-both, then by meaning, then by word; a prompt brings the best match in full and names up to five more by key and summary; with the model in use a match by word alone is only named unless the prompt names the memory (a hyphenated token); rank() lost its 4,000-character cap; the tool hook adds a lookup by meaning on every Bash command (commands every, the default the user asked for), on failures only (failed) or never (off), and at a failure matches what the command printed. Floors 0.40 (prompts, error text) and 0.45 (commands), set from the real store: plain commands such as git status score up to 0.5 against the memories about their tool. Decisions and what was rejected: a process per lookup, not a resident one (1.5 s is fine by the user; noted as the upgrade); pip --target into one directory, not a venv (this machine has no ensurepip); one memory in full, not two (two brought 3 more right memories and 8 more unrelated ones in full); no word matching on error text (a live run named two unrelated memories for 'command not found'). Verified: selftest with new cases (merge, summary, named, the two-long-memories case that the old cap dropped, deliver's output and seen marks); the quality gate; crew-recall setup run for real on this machine (28 s, 1.26 GB model, test lookup 2.4 s cold); the shipped hooks run end to end over the real store, 58 hook calls: a right memory in full for 16 of 19 prompts (14 by word alone), 24 of 26 right memories in full or named (22), 1 unrelated memory in full (3), nothing in full on 10 unrelated prompts (3), 3 of 4 commands and the 1 error text (2 of 5 together by word alone), median hook time 1.6 s; and a live headless session with --plugin-dir showing the wake-up line, the prompt's memory in full with five named, and the failure hook. Not verified: any machine but this one, a store other than the two used, behaviour under many sessions at once (the lock slots are untested under load), and macOS. Left alone: ck-88a (the tool trigger still fires on any token: on 24 plain commands it brought 20 memories in full by itself).

title: Pinned memories: key and summary of each at every wake-up, unpinned ones not listed
description: User: 'let's introduce a concept of "pinned" memories, which will always be injected into the session start' and then 'only keywords + summaries, not the full memories. un-pinned not listed at all. Build that.' Why: he does not care to see every memory at session start (the rest should arrive by prompt or tool call) and wants the wake-up as lean as possible.
design: bd stores a memory as key + text, no flags, so the pin is a line in the text, like Symptom: today: 'Pinned: <one-line summary>'. The wake-up prints 'key: summary' per pinned memory under one header line that still gives the total count and how the rest arrive; the topic counts are removed. Rejected: a key prefix (pin-...) because the key's topic is already the tool trigger; a separate pin list file because it would drift from the store and is one more thing in git; injecting the full text because the user said summaries only. The summary is written by the author in the Pinned line; an empty one falls back to the memory's first line. The section is capped so a wall of pins cannot push the rest of the wake-up over the 10,000-character hook cap, and it moves ahead of the seat file and diary so the cut at 9,500 bytes takes the diary's tail, not the pins. Subagents: not in scope (the user said session start); they keep getting tool and failure memories.

comments.author: siler
comments.text: Built, not committed, not released. hooks/memories.py: pinned() reads a line 'Pinned: <summary>' at the start of a line of a memory's text (a bare 'Pinned:' falls back to the memory's first other line; a summary is cut at 200 characters); index() now prints one header line with the count and how memories arrive, then '- key: summary' per pinned memory up to 1,500 characters, then '- and N more pinned, not shown'. The topic counts are gone and an unpinned memory is not listed. hooks/session-start.sh prints that block right after bd prime, ahead of the seat file and diary, so the 9,500-byte cut takes a long diary's tail and not the pins. PRIME.md (+180 bytes in every wake-up; copy refreshed in .beads/) and README.md say how to pin. Verified: selftest (two new assertions: summary, bare fallback, 'pinned:' inside a sentence is not a pin, a long summary is cut), dry runs of index with a stub bd (2 of 4 pinned; none pinned prints the header only; 30 long pins stop at 8 shown, 1,626 bytes in all), a dry run of session-start.sh in a scratch project showing the block between the rules and the seat section, and the full quality gate (plugin validate --strict, sh -n on every hook and bin script, ast parse, selftest): all pass. Not done: no live claude -p run (the path from hook stdout to context is unchanged), no memory in this repo is pinned yet (the user's choice which), subagents do not get the pinned list (he said session start). Also asked another project's seat, at the user's word, for a real memory store to test recall on; its copy will stay in the session scratch directory and out of this repo.

title: Pinned memories at wake-up; the rest recalled by meaning from the prompt or tool call, locally
description: User's brief (2026-11-09), after reading the survey (ck-6ft) and being told about 58 keys fit in the wake-up: 'I do not massively care about showing all the memories on session start - I want relevant memories to be fetched in based on a prompt or a tool call. Let's do it this way - let's introduce a concept of "pinned" memories, which will always be injected into the session start, with names of the memories or keywords. Then we need a very good search of the memories that are relevant to the prompt - I think we need to have some sort of semantic similarity measure. What can be used locally WITHOUT any external API calls?' Earlier in the same thread: 'I'm just not happy that we'll be relying on the authors of the memories to use specific keywords. It needs to be a little bit more fuzzy and semantic.' and 'We want to be as lean as possible.' This overrules the survey's option B (a full index at wake-up): he does not want every memory listed at session start.
design: Open, waiting on the user's choice. Facts in hand: bd stores a memory as key + text only (no flags), so a pin has to be a convention in the text or the key; no uv, pipx, ollama or llama-server on this machine; a selector through claude -p is an external API call and is out. Local candidates measured on a 15-note toy (see ck-6ft): recall terms written at save time and read by the existing FTS5 (15/15, 10 ms, no install); a small sentence transformer on ONNX Runtime (13-14/15 in the top 3, 0.3-0.4 s, 175 MB of packages plus a 23-90 MB model); static embeddings read with the standard library (9/15, 31 MB of model files). My reading of 'pinned ... with names of the memories or keywords', to be confirmed: a pinned memory's text is injected whole at every wake-up; unpinned ones are not listed.

comments.author: siler
comments.text: User (2026-11-09): 'pinned memories - only keywords + summaries, not the full memories. un-pinned not listed at all. Build that. Re. recall terms - more information please.' So: the wake-up lists a pinned memory's key and a summary, never its text; the topic counts go; recall terms are not approved yet, he asked for an explanation first.

comments.author: siler
comments.text: Tested on a real store shared by a seat on another project at the user's word (91 memories, mean 717 characters; 24 labelled cases: 19 prompts with 26 right memories, 5 commands or error texts; the copy stays in the session scratch directory). Results, in counts. Shipped rank(): a right memory for 17 of 19 prompts, 20 of 26 right memories, 27 other memories delivered alongside, 6 delivered on 10 unrelated prompts. With blind model-written Recall terms: 16, 18, 29, 9: worse. With the 4,000-character cap lifted: shipped 17 / 22 / 38 / 9, terms 18 / 22 / 48 / 14. MiniLM top 3 over a 0.30 floor: 17 / 19 / 23 / 1; adding MiniLM to the lexical result added no right memory. Why the shipped ranking missed 6 right memories: 3 ranked third, fourth and sixth but the character cap was full (all on the user's two real prompts; one memory is 3,434 characters), 2 matched a single word where the rule needs two, 1 shared no word. Commands and errors: the tool trigger found 2 of 8 right memories, 4 of 8 with MiniLM top 2 over 0.30, MiniLM alone top 3 found 5. So the toy result of ck-6ft (terms 1/15 -> 15/15) did not carry over: I withdrew the recall-terms recommendation and corrected the survey doc. What the real store points at instead: deliver by summary (full text for the best match, key + summary for the next ones, a cap by count not characters), and embeddings only where they showed a gain (command and error text). Caveat: 15 of the 19 prompts were written by a seat that knows the store, which favours word matching.

comments.author: siler
comments.text: User asked how large an embedding model is realistic on a CPU ('we are OK to download a few GB of model and use up a few seconds for the command lookup + CPU cycles'). Measured on this machine (8 threads, AVX-512, ONNX Runtime, one lookup in a fresh process) against the same real store (19 prompts / 26 right memories, 5 commands or errors / 8 right; 'floored' = top 3 above the highest similarity seen on 10 unrelated prompts, so nothing is delivered on those): all-MiniLM-L6-v2 23M, 0.09 GB: lookup 0.4-0.5 s, 0.2 GB RAM; floored 15 prompts / 16 right, commands 3 cases / 3 right. bge-base 110M, 0.44 GB: 0.9-1.0 s, 0.7 GB; floored 14 / 15, 3 / 3. bge-large 335M, 1.34 GB: 2.4-2.5 s, 2.1 GB; floored 14 / 16, 3 / 3. EmbeddingGemma 300M, 1.26 GB: 1.4-1.5 s, 0.7 GB; floored 18 / 21, 5 / 6. bge-m3 568M, 2.28 GB: 1.7 s, 1.8 GB; floored 18 / 19, 5 / 5. Qwen3-Embedding 0.6B, 2.41 GB: 2.3-2.4 s, 2.6 GB; floored 16 / 18, 3 / 3. For reference the shipped word matching: 17 prompts / 20 right with 6 memories delivered on the unrelated prompts, and the tool trigger 2 command cases / 2 right. So size did not buy quality here: the 300M model was best, and it is the first method that beats the shipped ranking on every column. Indexing the 91 memories once took 1 s to 65 s depending on the model. Not measured: models over 1B parameters (no ONNX files, llama.cpp not installed), quantized variants, a resident process. Caveats: 24 cases, single runs, the floor is tuned on the same 10 unrelated prompts, and my query prefixes may not be the best for every model.

title: The kit writes idleCompaction false into every crew project's .claude/settings.json
description: User: 'When session is started with crewkit initialised, we ALWAYS want the idleCompaction set to false. How do we achieve it with our plugin setup?' then 'Kit should write it per project, let's build this first.' A plugin cannot set it: the manifest's settings field honours only agent and subagentStatusLine (docs and binary, 2.1.310). A compaction replaces a seat's memory with a summary, which the kit exists to avoid, so the setting belongs to every adopted project.
design: Two writers, same rule. /crew:adopt writes .claude/settings.json with idleCompaction false (merging into an existing file). The SessionStart hook does the same whenever a project with crew/ lacks the key, so projects adopted before 1.3.1 get it at their next start; it prints one line so the seat commits the file. The merge is a python3 json load/dump that preserves other keys and leaves a file alone that is not valid JSON. The docs say a settings file created in the project's .claude/ is loaded in the same session. Rejected: a plugin settings.json (keys dropped at load), user-level settings on each machine (manual, not enforced by the kit). Also lands ck-a4v in the same hook: export.auto true -> false with a line to commit .beads/config.yaml.
close_reason: Released as 1.3.1 (tag crew--v1.3.1). The SessionStart hook merges idleCompaction=false into .claude/settings.json wherever it is missing and says so; /crew:adopt writes it at adoption. Verified in a scratch project (created, merged with other keys kept, silent when already false, invalid JSON and non-object left alone) and on this repo; strict gate passes. A plugin cannot set it itself, so this is per project and committed.

comments.author: siler
comments.text: Built, not released. hooks/session-start.sh merges idleCompaction=false into .claude/settings.json (python3 json; other keys kept; a file that is not valid JSON or not an object is left alone) and prints one 'crew:' line asking for the commit; the adopt skill writes it at adoption; README Files list, 1.3.1 changelog. Scratch-project tests: no .claude dir -> file created with the key; a file with permissions and idleCompaction true -> merged, permissions kept, false set; already false -> untouched and silent; invalid JSON and a JSON list -> untouched and silent; this repo as siler -> silent. Strict gate passes.

title: Prompt-hook memory matching injects mostly unrelated memories
description: User's brief (relayed by a seat on another project, 2026-10-26): the 1.3.0 UserPromptSubmit hook (hooks/memories.py match) injects mostly unrelated memories; research the ranking more widely before choosing a fix, then implement. Findings from that seat's replay of one session on a project with 47 memories: the script runs cleanly, but the query is an OR of the prompt's non-stop words and the only cut-off is relative to the best match (score > 0.4 * best), so when nothing really matches, the best hit is itself one common word and up to five memories ride in on it: 22 injected over six prompts, one relevant. Bead ids make it worse: the tokenizer splits <prefix>-<id> into two tokens and the prefix token is in 37 of 47 memories (every memory that cites a bead), so 'any more work on <prefix>-5x2?' matched 38 of 47 on 'any' plus the prefix. Other high-frequency tokens there are project-specific (the year, '10', 'page', the user's first name, 'run', 'qa'), so a fixed stop list cannot cover them. Also: a prompt resent with one more word burned its five matches on the first run and got the next five on the resend (once-per-context rule). Starting idea from that seat, not a spec: drop query words that occur in more than about a third of the memories, read from an fts5vocab table so it self-tunes per project; require a memory to match at least two query words when the prompt has two or more. Questions the user wants answered before choosing: an absolute score floor instead of the relative one; keeping the bead-id suffix token as an exact hit so a prompt naming a bead pulls memories citing it; what the 3x key weighting does; whether the 0.4 relative threshold earns its place; behaviour on a project with few memories.
design: Four rules in memories.py match, the rest unchanged (FTS5 porter, bm25 key 3x, rel 0.4, TOP 5, CAP 4000, once per context). (1) Document-frequency filter: a prompt word found in more than a third of the memories is dropped from the query, measured per project with a MATCH count over all memories, only when the project has at least 10 (below that a third is under three memories and the filter would eat everything). (2) Two-word rule: a memory is a candidate only if it matches at least two of the kept query terms, or the prompt had fewer than two terms. (3) Hyphenated tokens (bead ids like acme-1a2b, and words like crew-wake) become FTS5 phrase terms (adjacent tokens); a phrase hit qualifies a memory on its own, bypassing the df filter and the two-word rule, so a prompt naming a bead pulls the memory that cites it. (4) 'ok' joins the stop list. The table now indexes all memories (df over the full set) and seen keys are skipped at pick time. The relative cut-off is taken from the best qualifying candidate. A selftest subcommand with a fixed memory set checks the four rules and joins the quality gate. Rejected: an absolute score floor (fragile across projects and prompt lengths), a bigger fixed stop list (cannot know a project's own frequent tokens), changing the once-per-context rule for resends (noise removal makes the burn rare).
close_reason: Released as 1.3.2 (tag crew--v1.3.2). memories.py rank(): a prompt word in more than a third of the project's memories is dropped (from 10 memories up); a memory qualifies on two kept words, or on a hyphenated token matched as a phrase (bead ids), or when the prompt has one term; 'ok' is a stop word; rel 0.4, key 3x, TOP 5, CAP 4000, once per context unchanged. selftest in the quality gate. Verified by replay on a 55-memory project through the real hook (six noise prompts to zero, every real hit kept, a bead-naming prompt pulls the memories citing it, 0.26 s) and on the kit's own memories. Left out: an absolute score floor and any change to the once-per-context rule, as recorded in the comments.

comments.author: siler
comments.text: Research on the same 55-memory project (ranking variants replayed over 10 prompts: the relayed ones plus the earlier test prompts and three chit-chat prompts). (1) Cause confirmed: an OR query with a relative cut-off only; when nothing matches well, one common word carries up to five memories. The project's bead prefix sits in 46 of 55 memories and the year in 44; a fixed stop list cannot know them. (2) Document-frequency filter (drop a query word present in more than a third of the memories, measured per project with a MATCH count; disabled below 10 memories, where a third is under 3) removes the prefix and the year but by itself changes nothing: the remaining common word still carries five. (3) Requiring a memory to match at least two query words when the prompt has two or more is what removes the noise: the two bead-id prompts and 'yes go ahead and commit it' go from five injected to none, every prompt with a real hit keeps it in the same place, and the curl prompt still returns exactly its one memory. (4) The 0.4 relative cut-off earns its place: without it the curl prompt returns five instead of one and weak tails come back everywhere. (5) Key weight 3x vs 1x: only small reorderings within the relevant set; keep 3x. (6) An absolute floor is fragile: a real single-word hit scores about -3.4 while noise on long prompts scores -2 to -4, and scores shift with the memory count; the two-word rule is structural and self-tuning. (7) Bead ids: the tokenizer splits <prefix>-<id> into two tokens; with the two-word rule a prompt naming a bead would lose the memory that cites it when nothing else matches, so a bead-shaped token should become a phrase query ('prefix id', adjacent tokens) that counts as a hit on its own. (8) Single-word prompts: 'ok' matches one memory on 'ok'; add it to the stop list; a lone rare word like 'gzip' should still find its memory and does. (9) Small projects: on the kit's own two memories the two-word rule keeps the one prompt that matters. (10) The resend burn (a prompt resent with one more word got the next five) mostly disappears once noise is not injected; no change to the once-per-context rule proposed. Proposal, about 15 lines in memories.py: df filter + two-word rule + bead-id phrase + 'ok' in STOP; keep rel 0.4, kw 3x, TOP 5, CAP 4000.

comments.author: siler
comments.text: Built, not released. memories.py: rank() holds the four rules, match() calls it, selftest subcommand (12 fixed memories, 8 assertions: bead id as phrase, df filter, two-word rule, single rare term, chit-chat, no tail, seen keys, df filter off below 10) is in the quality gate. Replay on the 55-memory project through the real hook: the two bead-status prompts for beads no memory cites went from 5 injected to 0; a prompt naming a bead two memories cite returns those two; 'yes go ahead and commit it' and 'ok' go from 5 and 1 to 0; the bd-list, crewkit-memory, compare-table, playwright, curl and 'gzip?' prompts keep their hits in the same order (the compare-table prompt drops its weakest fifth); 'what does the dev-server need for curl?' finds its memory by the phrase. On the kit's own two memories 'why was the hook output cut off?' now returns only the cap memory (before: both). 0.26 s per prompt, unchanged. README, 1.3.2 changelog, gate line updated.

title: SessionStart hook output exceeds Claude Code's inline limit: the seat section is cut off
description: A seat on another project woke with crew-wake and ran a whole session without its seat identity. The SessionStart hook printed 24.5KB / 204 lines; Claude Code did not inline it but wrote 'Output too large (24KB). Full output saved to: <session dir>/tool-results/hook-....txt' with a 2KB preview that ended inside PRIME.md's Commands section. The seat section (# You are <seat>, SEAT.md, last diary entry, beads in progress, inbox) started at byte 20,756 and was never read. Layout of the output: PRIME.md 3.2KB, then '## Persistent Memories (29)' 17.6KB (72%, printed by bd prime, grows with every bd remember), then the seat section 3.8KB. CLAUDE.md's health check ('context did not start with # Beads workflow') passed because the first 2KB was exactly that. User's brief: investigate and present options with trade-offs, do not implement yet. Preference stated: PRIME.md and the seat section first, memories last, so a truncation only ever costs memories. Things to check: whether bd prime can print the rules without the memories; whether memories should be capped in the hook (bytes, count, keys only); the seat line as the very first line as cheap insurance; whether hookSpecificOutput.additionalContext has the same size limit as plain stdout; the actual inline threshold on this Claude Code version and whether it is documented; PRIME.md's 'append your diary entry if you have a seat' reads as optional, and the CLAUDE.md health check should look for the seat line.
design: Shipped as 1.3.0. SessionStart: the seat line is the first line of output, then 'if this output was saved to a file, read it', then bd prime --no-memories (falls back to bd prime on an older bd), the seat section, and a topic index of memory keys instead of their text; the whole output is built in a function and measured, and cut at 9,500 bytes with a note if a seat's files ever push it over, so the seat can never be lost to the 10,000-character cap. Memories: a new UserPromptSubmit hook (prompt-submit.sh -> memories.py match) dumps bd memories --json once per prompt, matches the prompt's words of four or more characters minus stopwords against key and value, ranks by distinct matches, injects the top 5 under 4,000 characters as additionalContext, and injects each key once per context (a seen-file per session id in TMPDIR, cleared by the SessionStart hook, which fires on every new context). PRIME.md states the key convention <topic>-<slug> and that memories arrive with the prompt. Rejected: capping bd prime's memories (alphabetical survivors, finding 10); keys only in the hook (an index of topics is smaller and scales further); separate SessionStart hook commands per part (order in context not guaranteed, memories still over the cap); embedding search (bd has none, keyword match is the lazy version with a known ceiling).
close_reason: Released as 1.3.0 (tag crew--v1.3.0). Shipped: seat line first in the SessionStart output plus a read-the-saved-file line, bd prime --no-memories with a fallback, a topic index of memories instead of their text, the whole output measured and cut at 9,500 bytes; a UserPromptSubmit hook (prompt-submit.sh, memories.py) that injects the memories matching the prompt via SQLite FTS5 with Porter stems and BM25, five at most, 4,000 characters, each once per context, weak matches dropped at 40% of the best score; PRIME.md's key convention and seat check; the health-check wording in the adopt template and this repo's instructions. Verified: strict gate; direct hook runs for seat, no seat, new seat; the prompt hook's seen-file round trip; matches on a project with 30 memories; an end-to-end claude -p session with --plugin-dir in which the model quoted the seat line and the injected memory's key. Left out: semantic search (embeddings), recorded as the upgrade path in the bead and README.

comments.author: siler
comments.text: Findings (Claude Code 2.1.301, bd 1.3.0). (1) The inline limit is 10,000 characters per hook string, preview 2,000 chars; found in the binary (persist function: threshold 1e4, preview 2000) and documented at code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks: 'A hook's additionalContext, systemMessage, and initialUserMessage strings, and its plain stdout, are capped at 10,000 characters ... this cap has no setting or environment variable to raise it ... Claude can read the file, but Claude Code doesn't ask it to.' (2) hookSpecificOutput.additionalContext goes through the same function with the same default threshold, measured per field. Live test: a 24KB hook in both forms, model asked for the first and last marker line: first seen, last not seen, both forms. (3) bd prime has --no-memories, --memories-only, --max-memories N, --max-memory-chars N (entries only, header and banner excluded) and --hook-json; its help says 'hosts truncate silently'. Caps are ALPHABETICAL, not newest first, with a banner 'N more memories are not shown ... bd memories <keyword>'. bd memories --json is key->content, no dates, so newest-first is not available from the CLI. (4) bd's default template starts with a banner '[bd prime] If this output is truncated by your host, read the full persisted hook output before continuing'; a custom .beads/PRIME.md (ours) replaces that banner, so the kit removed bd's own safeguard. (5) Sizes: PRIME.md 3,159 B; seat section 2.1 KB (kit seats) to 3.8 KB (the affected seat); memories average ~600 B each, 30 entries = 18 KB; keys-only listing of 31 memories = 1.3 KB. Budget under 10,000 with order PRIME+seat+memories: about 3-4.5 KB for memories, i.e. 5-7 entries.

comments.author: siler
comments.text: More findings. (6) Boundary confirmed live: a 9,977-byte plain-stdout hook was inlined whole (both markers seen); 10,489 bytes was persisted (last marker not seen). (7) Over the cap the output is not cut at 10,000: the WHOLE string is replaced by the path plus the first 2,000 chars. PRIME.md alone is 3,159 bytes, so reordering to PRIME, seat, memories does NOT save the seat on its own: a 24 KB output would still show only the first 2 KB of PRIME.md. The seat survives only if the total stays under 10,000, or if the seat line sits inside the first 2,000 chars. (8) The inlined note reads 'Output too large (25.1KB). Full output saved to: <path>' then 'Preview (first 2KB):' and does not ask the model to read the file. (9) The hook result is prefixed 'SessionStart:startup hook success:' in context, and other plugins' SessionStart hooks can precede ours, so a 'context starts with' health check is already not literal. (10) Memory dates are not reachable: bd memories --json is key->content and bd sql is 'not yet supported in embedded mode', so newest-first needs an upstream bd change.

comments.author: siler
comments.text: Options presented to the user (not implemented): A. Reorder in session-start.sh: bd prime --no-memories, seat section, then bd prime --memories-only; two bd calls. On its own it does not save the seat (finding 7). B. Keep the total under 10,000: measure what the script has printed so far and give the rest to bd prime --memories-only --max-memory-chars <remaining>; bd prints the elision banner. Alphabetical survivors, 5-7 entries at today's sizes. C. Seat line as the first line of output, plus a one-line 'if this output was saved to a file, read it before anything else' (bd's own banner, which our custom PRIME.md dropped). Insurance inside the 2,000-char preview. D. Keys-only memory listing (1.3 KB for 31 keys) with 'bd memories <key>' to read one; scales to hundreds, costs the always-present promise. E. Split into separate SessionStart hook commands (rules / seat / memories), each measured on its own; buys decoupling but memories over 10K are still persisted, and multi-hook order in context is not guaranteed. F. Wording: PRIME.md 'append your diary entry if you have a seat' -> check echo $SEAT and if set but no '# You are' section in context, the wake-up output was cut; health check in CLAUDE.md/adopt to look for the seat line. Newest-first is not possible from bd's CLI today (finding 10).

comments.author: siler
comments.text: User asked whether alphabetical order is odd. Checked every place bd exposes memories: bd memories --json (key->value), bd recall --json (found/key/schema_version/value), bd export --include-memories ({_type:memory,key,value}). None carries a timestamp, so bd stores no date for memories and no client can order them by age. Alphabetical is the only order bd has. Side finding: bd export excludes memories by default, so .beads/issues.jsonl carries none and the kit's SessionEnd hook and handoff export leave them machine-local; filed as a follow-up.

comments.author: siler
comments.text: User: 'We need a system that scales with many, many memories.' Proposed design (not implemented): wake-up carries an index, content arrives when relevant. (1) SessionStart: seat first, total guarded under 10,000, bd prime --no-memories, then a topic index of memory keys (distinct first word of the key with counts, a few hundred bytes at any count) and 'bd memories <word> reads them'. (2) UserPromptSubmit hook: one bd memories --json dump (0.2 s measured at 30 entries, search is case-insensitive substring over key and value), match the prompt's distinctive words against key and value in-process, rank by matches, inject the top few as additionalContext under a ~4 KB cap. Scales to thousands with one bd call per prompt. (3) Hygiene: PRIME.md states keys as <topic>-<slug> so the index and manual search stay meaningful; ck-eoq makes the store travel with the repo. Replaces bd's own memory section (always --no-memories). Trade-offs: keyword matching, not semantic; ~0.3 s per prompt; relevance decided by the hook, misses cost one manual search. Alternative trigger considered: PreToolUse on Edit/Write/Read injecting memories that name the touched path; more precise for code gotchas, fires often, kept as a later addition.

title: Tool memories fire on any token of a command, not on the programs it runs
description: Found while researching ck-6ft. The PreToolUse path (memories.py tools()) matches a memory's key topic against every whitespace-separated token of the Bash command, its basename and that minus its extension. Three false deliveries seen in one day: a memory keyed release- arrived because the word 'release' stood inside a heredoc of test data; two keyed claude- arrived on 'Claude' in a grep pattern and '.claude' in a path; and one keyed claude- arrived on a bd create whose description text held 'claude.ai' (splitext turns claude.ai into claude). Each wrong delivery spends context and marks the memory as seen, so it will not come again when its tool really runs in that context. Why it matters now: the research found that deterministic triggers are the part of the kit worth keeping, and they are only worth keeping if they are precise.
design: Not decided. Candidates: match only the command words (the first token of each simple command after splitting on | ; && || and after env assignments and wrappers such as timeout, nohup, sudo, env, xargs), drop heredoc bodies and quoted strings before tokenising, and stop stripping extensions from tokens that are not paths to a script. The selftest already covers 'cat qa/notes.md' as a non-match; add the three cases above.
close_reason: programs() in hooks/memories.py reads only the programs a command runs: the first word of each simple command (split on newlines, pipes, ;, &, &&, ||, braces, backticks and $( ), after heredoc bodies, quoted strings and redirections are removed), past FOO=bar assignments and the wrappers sudo, doas, env, nohup, time, timeout N, xargs, exec, command, builtin, nice, setsid, stdbuf, watch; an interpreter (python, sh, bash, node, ruby, perl and kin) also counts its first non-flag word, so python3 runtests.py and ./runtests.sh both yield runtests. Verified by the selftest with the three cases from this bug (a heredoc body, a quoted claude.ai text, a grep pattern plus a .claude path), wrappers, a substitution, and the old cases; ls qa no longer fires the qa- memories, which the selftest now asserts the other way. Shipped in 1.6.0.

title: Research: how other agents' memory works, to make memory recall fuzzier than author keywords
description: User's brief (2026-11-09), following the 1.5.0 work on tool memories: 'I would like to perform deep research on how different memory models for existing agents work. What does ChatGPT do? What does Claude do? What does Open Claude do? What does Hermes agent do? Our case is a little bit more specific on the project coding level, but I'm sure we can get some learnings from it, simplify our setup, and make it even more powerful. Overall, I'm just not happy that we'll be relying on the authors of the memories to use specific keywords. It needs to be a little bit more fuzzy and semantic. Maybe at some point in the very future we would need to turn our attention to some sort of semantic modelling, but let's do this detailed research into the major players. I think Devin was one of them. A thorough research, please. Maybe a doc as an artefact so I can review it more easily.' Deliverable: a research doc (a claude.ai doc artifact) the user reviews; no kit code changes in this bead. Why: recall today depends on the memory's author choosing the key topic and words a later prompt or command happens to share.
design: Read 'Open Claude' as OpenClaw (the open-source personal agent) and 'Hermes agent' as the Nous Research one; said so in the doc. Research fanned out to subagents, one per system, notes kept in the session scratchpad and not in this public repo. The doc ends with options for the kit and a yes/no for the user, not a decision taken for him.
close_reason: Delivered a research doc (a private claude.ai doc artifact, 'How agents remember: a survey of memory systems'; its link is kept out of this public repo and is in the seat's local memory). Sections: bottom line, the kit today, ChatGPT and Codex, Claude, OpenClaw, Hermes Agent, Devin, other coding agents, memory frameworks and the evidence, side by side with a drawn map, patterns, options for the kit, sources. It ends with four options and one yes/no for the user: build 'recall terms at save time' plus 'a description per memory and the full index at wake-up', with the tool-trigger fix (ck-88a) and a recall log; a selector model and local embeddings are costed and left. Verified: every section is filled (outline read back), the drawing was looked at rendered and one overflowing label fixed, and the two kit rows of the measurement table were run here against hooks/memories.py. Not verified: the researchers' quotes came through a fetch tool that returns extracts, OpenAI's own pages refused the fetch, and the embedding and selector figures were run by a research subagent and not re-run by me. No kit code changed. The research notes and test scripts are in the session scratchpad and will not outlive it.

comments.author: siler
comments.text: Findings so far (5 of 6 research threads back; notes in the session scratchpad, the doc is a claude.ai doc artifact). 1) Almost nobody uses embeddings for memory recall: ChatGPT, Codex, Claude Code, Devin, Copilot, Cursor document none; only one open-source personal agent's search leg and another's optional plugins do. Fuzzy recall is a model reading short text: everything injected under a hard cap, or an index of one-line descriptions. 2) Codex memories v2 (Sept 2026) deleted its keyword layer for an injected index of 'one semantic sentence explaining what it contains and when it matters'; Devin folded trigger-based Knowledge into Skills (description in context). 3) Claude Code auto memory has a reverse-engineered side query: a small model reads name+description of each memory file and returns up to 5, told to match on what the question is about, not keyword overlap. 4) A passive listing alone is unreliable (one third-party test: skills fire ~50% unaided, 100% when a hook forces a check). 5) Background curation is everywhere and unattended curation has deleted user data in two projects. 6) This repo holds 6 memories, 2,219 characters: at that size the survey's own advice is to inject an index, not retrieve. Premises that turned out stale: Devin Knowledge is deprecated; Copilot expiry is 90 days, not 28; the Hermes session-search summariser and pre-compression flush were removed. Researchers were told not to write to bd (six long reports would bury the bead); this comment stands in for theirs.

comments.author: siler
comments.text: All six threads back. Added since the last comment: (a) memory frameworks: for a store that fits in context no published result shows a heavyweight architecture beating full context or plain files with search; one framework vendor's own table has full context ahead of its memory layer; benchmark scores move 26 points with the grading prompt alone; a keyword-only agent collapsed on paraphrased queries in a database vendor's test (29.7% against 87.1%). (b) Hook facts checked against the Claude Code docs: prompt-type and agent-type hooks return only allow/block, so a selector model at prompt time must be a command hook that starts claude -p itself (blocking, 30 s default timeout, undocumented pattern); each hook string has its own 10,000-character cap; SubagentStart context reaches the subagent. (c) Measured in this session on a researcher's toy set (15 notes, 15 prompts sharing no content words with their note, 5 no-match prompts): the kit's shipped rank() delivered the right note for 1 of 15; with a line of model-written recall terms appended to each note, 15 of 15, with 6 other notes riding along and nothing delivered on the 5 no-match prompts. Static embeddings found 9 of 15 in the top 3, a small transformer 13 to 14, a small-model selector over keys 15 of 15. Toy: the order of the options holds, the sizes do not. (d) The tool trigger fired wrongly three times during this work: ck-88a.

title: Memories about a tool's behaviour arrive with the first command that runs the tool
description:
Brief from a sister seat on another project, relayed as the user's ask (2026-11-06). Memories (bd remember) about how a tool behaves in this environment never surface when they are needed, because retrieval matches memory text against the user's prompt only, and the moment such a memory matters is a tool call or a tool result, not a prompt. The user wants an extensible mechanism, not a one-off rule in CLAUDE.md.

The case (a Django project, dev server on a local port): the task was a UI bug in a mobile overlay; every prompt word was UI. The seat ran curl against the dev server to warm a page cache; curl hung until its timeout, several times (120 s, 400 s, 500 s, then a verification loop of 90 x 900 s), while the server log showed a 200 within seconds. A memory describing exactly this existed, written by the same seat a month earlier (key dev-server-curl-needs-gzip: curl must send Accept-Encoding gzip, otherwise a string-replacement middleware leaves a stale Content-Length and curl waits until its timeout). The wake-up listed it only as 'dev 1'. It never arrived with the prompt (no shared words); it arrived 23 hours later, attached to a background-task notification whose text happened to match. The verification loop had burnt most of a day. A second instance the same day: the auto-memory note 'first render takes ~30 s' was reachable and pushed the wrong reading further; nothing in either store was wrong, the right one was unreachable.

Why it is structural: memories about a tool's behaviour here (curl needs --compressed; a background docker run --rm trips the harness check; Playwright WebKit crashes alongside the suite; a simulator device has no overflow at 402pt) are keyed by the tool or the symptom, neither of which appears in a prompt. The author wants it to fire on the command or the failure, and there is no place to say so. The seat-habit fix (look up memories when a tool misbehaves) needs the seat to recognise misbehaviour; here the server log contradicted the reading and the seat still did not look.

Directions the seat listed, to evaluate: (a) match on tool use, a PreToolUse hook for Bash on the command's binaries and hostnames, PostToolUse on the result (exit 124, timeout, Connection refused); (b) let the author declare the trigger, a trigger field or a topic-prefix convention (curl-, docker-) the hooks map to binaries; (c) a pinned tier printed in full at wake-up; (d) print the keys of tool topics at wake-up instead of counts; (e) whatever fires on tool use stays small, dedupes per session, never fires on every Bash call, and reaches subagents. Constraint: bd remember stays the single store; the gap is retrieval.
design: Taken, three parts in one mode of hooks/memories.py (tool), behind hooks/tool-use.sh. (1) The author declares the trigger in the key's topic (curl-, docker-, playwright-): a PreToolUse hook on Bash injects the memories whose topic is a whole token of the command, the basename of a path token, or that without its extension, as additionalContext; once per context through the same seen-file as the prompt path, with a per-subagent file (session_id-agent_id). (2) A failure is the moment such a memory matters: a PostToolUseFailure hook on Bash sends the failed command's tool memories once more per context, unless they arrived with that very call (the seen-file holds marks next to keys: @<tool_use_id>:<key> and !<key>); a user's interrupt is skipped. (3) For memories keyed by an area whose trigger is the failure and not a tool, the author declares it in the text with a line 'Symptom: phrase; phrase', matched as a case-insensitive substring of the error text; phrases under four characters count for nothing. Facts checked on 2.1.319: PreToolUse and PostToolUseFailure accept additionalContext and fire in subagents with agent_id; a non-zero exit and the harness timeout fire PostToolUseFailure with error = 'Exit code N' plus the output; so the failure hook costs nothing on successful commands. Cost: bd memories --json before every Bash call, 0.15 s measured, marked ponytail in tool-use.sh (cache per session if it shows). Rejected: matching the memory body against the command text or the error text with rank() (a command line is flags and URLs; error output is long and wordy, so a test failure dump would pull in unrelated memories; stems miss, timeout against timed out); matching any hyphenated word of the key rather than the topic (keys carry filler words such as copy, output, prime that are also command tokens); a separate trigger field (bd remember has key and text only, so the declaration lives in one of them); a pinned tier printed at wake-up (does not scale; the index line 'curl 1' already shows a tool topic exists, and a git- or bd- topic is in effect pinned); hostnames as triggers (no memory asks for it). Not covered: a command that exits zero while its output shows the problem (needs a scan of every call's output), background tasks (their notifications pass the prompt match only), a hyphenated tool name such as docker-compose as a topic.
close_reason: Shipped in 1.5.0: memories keyed by a tool (curl-, docker-, a script by its name without extension) arrive with the first Bash command of a context that runs the tool, in subagents too; a failed command brings its tool's memories once more per context; a memory with a 'Symptom: phrase; phrase' line arrives when a failed command's error contains a phrase. New hooks/tool-use.sh on PreToolUse and PostToolUseFailure (Bash), a tool mode in memories.py, the rule in PRIME.md, README and CHANGELOG. Verified by the selftest (16 new asserts over both parts), the quality gate, dry runs against this repo's store and a stub store, two read-only probes by a sister seat against a real project's store (first part, before and after re-keying its memories), and a live headless session on 2.1.319 with --plugin-dir (both hooks, four calls, the model quoted the expected memories). Left out on purpose: lexical matching of command or error text, symptoms in the output of a command that exits zero, background tasks beyond the prompt match of their notifications, hostnames and hyphenated tool names as topics, caching bd memories --json (0.15 s before every Bash call).

comments.author: siler
comments.text: The sister seat probed hooks/tool-use.sh read-only against its project's store with ten commands and fresh session ids: after re-keying its two tool memories by the tool (curl-..., pkill-...), curl in three forms and pkill -f each gave exactly their memory; git status gave its four git- memories, bd show its two bd- ones, ls qa four qa- ones; its test-runner wrapper, its manage wrapper and docker logs gave nothing. Before the re-key the curl and pkill rows gave nothing: the trigger is the key alone. Three findings: (1) a script with an extension never matched its topic (./runner.sh tokenises to runner.sh), so memories about a test-runner wrapper could not fire on it; fixed, the basename without its extension is a token too, with a selftest row. (2) A tool every context runs (bd, git) makes its topic a pinned tier: its memories arrive with the first bd or git command of every context. Kept as a property of the convention and written into PRIME and the README: right for a shared-checkout rule, wrong for a memory about a later step. (3) It left its headless Playwright memories area-keyed on purpose, since their tool is docker and the first docker command of a context is usually logs or compose, not the Playwright run: the author choosing the trigger is the design working. Known limit left out: a hyphenated tool name (docker-compose) cannot be a topic, since the topic ends at the first hyphen.

comments.author: siler
comments.text: Sister seat re-probed after the extension fix: its test-runner wrapper now fires its three runner memories; nothing else changed. One side effect it accepts: a test label that equals an area topic (./runner.sh test <app>) brings that area's memory, by the documented bare-token rule; a seat running an app's tests getting that app's memory reads as right. Wrappers with no keys fire nothing. Nothing further needed from its side.

comments.author: siler
comments.text: User asked how to also match on failure symptoms (2026-11-09). Checked in a throwaway headless session on 2.1.319 with logging hooks: a Bash call with a non-zero exit and one killed by the harness timeout both fire PostToolUseFailure, not PostToolUse; its input carries tool_input.command, duration_ms, is_interrupt and error ('Exit code 3' plus the stderr text; 'Exit code 143' plus 'Command timed out after 1s'); additionalContext printed by that hook reached the model after both failures. A successful call fires PostToolUse with stdout and stderr and no exit code. So a failure hook costs nothing on successful commands, and the earlier design note (symptoms need PostToolUse on every call) was wrong for failures. Options put to the user: (1) a failed command re-sends its tool's memories once per context, no new convention; (2) an author-declared 'Symptom:' line in the body, matched as a phrase in the error text, for area-keyed memories; (3) lexical match of the error text against bodies, rejected as noisy; (4) symptoms in exit-0 output or background tasks, not covered by a failure hook. No code changed; waiting for the user's decision.

comments.author: siler
comments.text: User (2026-11-09): yes, build both into 1.5.0: a failed command brings its tool's memories back, and an author-declared Symptom line matched against the error text.

comments.author: siler
comments.text: Verified the failure path: selftest (four new asserts: a declared phrase in the error, case and closing full stop, no phrase or seen gives nothing, symptom hits first and each key once); a nine-step dry run of tool-use.sh and prompt-submit.sh by absolute path against a stub store (first curl injects at PreToolUse; that same call failing injects nothing; a later curl failure injects it again under the failure header; a third nothing; a 'Target crashed' error with no tool injects the Symptom memory, in capitals too; again nothing; an interrupt nothing; a matching prompt in the same session nothing, in a fresh one the memory); a live headless session on 2.1.319 loading the kit with --plugin-dir in a scratch project with the stub store: four Bash calls, the model quoted curl-dev-gzip under the PreToolUse header after the first curl, headless-webkit under the failure header after the 'Target crashed' failure, curl-dev-gzip under the failure header after a later failed curl, and none after its repeat. The quality gate passes. hooks.json keeps its layout: 16 added lines. One slip while testing: rm -f /tmp/crew-mem-* by glob removed every running seat's seen-file on this machine, so each may receive once more a memory it already had; nothing else is lost.

title: Seats set the handoff title when they close a bead: the Titles rule reads as 'finished = handoff'
description: User (2026-11-03): "The titles seems to be erroneously being changed to 'handoff' mid work. Check with sharon from 42q and zelenka from subs, it happened to them. See what we can do to mitigate this." Transcripts: both seats ran 'crew-title handoff' in the same command as 'bd close' of the bead they had just finished, mid-session, with no handoff asked for (zelenka 2026-11-02 17:25, sharon 2026-11-03 11:01); roy's at 11:02 came from the handoff skill and was right. Zelenka's own diagnosis to the user (11-03 09:25): 'The crew Titles rule says the handoff ends with crew-title handoff, and when I closed the bead I ran it in the same command, as if closing the bead meant the session was ending.' Shipped in 1.4.0 (ck-gz3).
design: Three guards, since the wording alone is a bet on the seat's reading (user, 11-03: 'see sharon - seems to happen a lot'; sharon's label stayed handoff through 25 minutes of new work after one reflex at bead close). (1) PRIME.md Titles: a closed bead or a delivered report changes nothing; handoff is the skill's alone. (2) crew-title refuses the word handoff unless CREW_HANDOFF=1, which only the handoff skill's step 5 sets; the refusal text names the rule and gives no override, so a reflex run does nothing and exits 1. (3) The UserPromptSubmit hook reads the session registry (~/.claude/sessions/*.json, current name only) and, when the label is <session>:handoff, prints a one-line reminder to set the word; this also covers the user carrying on after a real handoff. (4) crew-title types the /rename line with -l and a separate Enter and waits up to 6 s for the registry's current name before claiming the label. Rejected: a hook that renames by itself (typing into the input from a hook races the user's prompt); a refusal keyed on the diary (a seat may write the diary early).
close_reason: Released as 1.4.1: PRIME.md Titles reworded (a closed bead changes nothing, handoff is the skill's alone); crew-title refuses the word handoff without CREW_HANDOFF=1, which only the handoff skill's step 5 sets; the prompt hook reminds a seat whose registry label still says handoff to set its word; crew-title types /rename literally with a separate Enter and confirms the registry's current name before claiming the label. Verified live on this session: refusal, skill rename, hook reminder present only while :handoff, restore within 1 s; gate green. Cause of zelenka's one lost rename not established; the registry check now reports it instead of claiming success. Running seats need a restart.

comments.author: siler
comments.text: Findings from the transcripts and registry (read directly; the seats were not woken): (1) zelenka 11-02 17:25 and sharon 11-03 11:01 each ran 'crew-title handoff' inside the same command as 'bd close', no handoff asked; roy's 11:02 came from the handoff skill. Root cause is the Titles wording 'The handoff ends with crew-title handoff', read as 'finished means handoff' (zelenka's own words to the user, 11-03 09:25). (2) zelenka's correction 'crew-title jsblock' at 09:25:33 reported 'label ...' but the typed /rename never reached the session: no '❯ /rename' line in the pane scrollback, no rename in the registry, and the Bash tool took 1m56s for a sub-second script (the other seven calls on record took 0-2 s). Cause of the lost keystrokes not established. Fix: PRIME.md Titles says a closed bead changes nothing and handoff is the skill's alone; crew-title types the line with -l and a separate Enter and waits up to 6 s for the registry's current name (not formerNames, which fooled a first grep) before claiming the label, else prints the /rename fallback.

comments.author: siler
comments.text: Tested 11-03 on this session (Claude Code 2.1.312, tmux 3.4): bare 'crew-title handoff' refused, exit 1, window and registry untouched; CREW_HANDOFF=1 renamed both to handoff; the prompt hook printed the Title reminder only while the registry said :handoff and nothing before or after; crew-title titles restored both within 1 s. Gate green. Not released yet.

title: Seats keep the tab title and the Remote Control label up to date: <seat>:<word>
description: User's brief (2026-10-29, relayed by the seat of another project that built and tested the patch): "every seat should keep the tab title up to date. A fresh session would get <name>:new. Then as we work on something, we would add a single word describing the work, such as tealc:abandon or tealc:navfix. Then as part of handoff, change to <name>:handoff. This word suffix should be also added to the claude remote control label, right after the four digit identifier." He chose ':' as the separator on the label (<prefix>_<seat>_<id>:<word>), had the patch built and tested there, and handed it to the kit for integration; version bump, CHANGELOG wording and the release are the kit's.
design: Taken: the tested patch as sent, 6 files. New bin/crew-title <word>: tmux rename-window -t $TMUX_PANE <seat>:<word>, then /rename <session>:<word> typed into the session's own pane with tmux send-keys. /rename is the only road a session has to its own Remote Control label (no tool, no mid-session hook field; SessionStart's sessionTitle applies only at startup, resume and fork). Guard: the last '❯' line of the pane is the input box; empty, it holds a no-break space or the 'Try ...' placeholder; anything else is a draft of the user's, so the label is left alone and the /rename line printed. crew-wake names the window <seat>:new, launches with --name/--remote-control <name>:new, exports CREW_SESSION and puts the kit's bin on PATH (readlink of $0, so the symlink install works): no install step. rename-window without -t renames the attached client's current window, not the one the command runs in, hence -t everywhere. title: Semantic search for memories: embeddings behind the FTS5 match

When a project passes a few hundred memories and misses show up, the upgrade is embeddings: embed each memory once into a cache under .beads/ keyed by content hash, embed the prompt per submit, rank by cosine in plain Python, same cap and seen-file. Easiest provider is an embeddings API (Voyage AI, which Anthropic's docs point to, or OpenAI) with an API key in the environment and the FTS5 match as the fallback when the key or network is missing; a local static model (model2vec) is the no-key option at the cost of the kit's first non-stdlib dependency. value: A live check of the kit's hooks without a release: a scratch project with crew/, a stub bd on PATH that answers 'memories --json' from a file and exits 0 otherwise, then claude -p '<the Bash calls to make; quote the hook context after each>' --plugin-dir <kit repo> --allowedTools Bash --model haiku < /dev/null. In dry runs call the hook scripts by absolute path (they cd to CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR first). Never rm /tmp/crew-mem-* by glob: those are every running seat's seen-files; remove the test session's own.

A session's name lives in ~/.claude/sessions/<pid>.json (name, nameSource, formerNames; tmux pane too) and, once renamed, in <project session dir>/custom-title.json; ps still shows the launch --name. /rename typed into the pane (crew-title) updates both within a few seconds, busy or idle.
A SessionStart hook only adds context; it cannot start a turn. Anything a seat must do at wake-up without the user typing needs crew-wake's initial prompt (see ck-hmi).

Claude Code inlines a hook's output only up to 10,000 characters per string (plain stdout, and each of additionalContext / systemMessage / initialUserMessage separately); over that it saves the text to <session dir>/tool-results/hook-*.txt and inlines a 2,000-char preview with the path, without telling the model to read it. Not configurable (checked 2.1.301 and the hooks docs). Every byte the SessionStart hook prints must fit under that; the seat line goes first (see ck-6l5).

PreToolUse, PostToolUse and PostToolUseFailure hooks accept hookSpecificOutput.additionalContext (shown to the model alongside the tool result, not before the tool runs) and fire inside subagents, with agent_id and agent_type in the hook input next to session_id. A Bash call with a non-zero exit or a harness timeout fires PostToolUseFailure, not PostToolUse: its input has tool_input.command and error ('Exit code N' plus the output; 'Command timed out after Ns'), no tool_response. Docs plus a logged headless run at 2.1.319 (ck-7d3).

Before a release commit that changes PRIME.md, refresh the project's copy: cp PRIME.md .beads/PRIME.md (the SessionStart hook does it only at the next start, so the 1.3.0 commit shipped a stale .beads/PRIME.md that caught up in 1.3.1).
